{{one source|date=June 2020}}

In mathematics, specifically in [[functional analysis]] and [[order theory]], a '''topological vector lattice''' is a [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] [[topological vector space]] (TVS) <math>X</math> that has a [[partial order]] <math>\,\leq\,</math> making it into [[vector lattice]] that possesses a neighborhood base at the origin consisting of [[solid set]]s.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=234–242}} 
Ordered vector lattices have important applications in [[spectral theory]].

== Definition ==

If <math>X</math> is a vector lattice then by '''the vector lattice operations''' we mean the following maps:
# the three maps <math>X</math> to itself defined by <math>x \mapsto|x |</math>, <math>x \mapsto x^+</math>, <math>x \mapsto x^{-}</math>, and
# the two maps from <math>X \times X</math> into <math>X</math> defined by <math>(x, y) \mapsto \sup_{} \{ x, y \}</math> and<math>(x, y) \mapsto \inf_{} \{ x, y \}</math>. 
If <math>X</math> is a TVS over the reals and a vector lattice, then <math>X</math> is locally solid if and only if (1) its positive cone is a [[normal cone (functional analysis)|normal cone]], and (2) the vector lattice operations are continuous.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=234–242}} 

If <math>X</math> is a vector lattice and an [[ordered topological vector space]] that is a [[Fréchet space]] in which the positive cone is a [[normal cone (functional analysis)|normal cone]], then the lattice operations are continuous.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=234–242}} 

If <math>X</math> is a [[topological vector space]] (TVS) and an [[ordered vector space]] then <math>X</math> is called '''locally solid''' if <math>X</math> possesses a neighborhood base at the origin consisting of [[solid set]]s.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=234–242}} 
A '''topological vector lattice''' is a [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] TVS <math>X</math> that has a [[partial order]] <math>\,\leq\,</math> making it into [[vector lattice]] that is locally solid.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=234–242}} 

== Properties ==

Every topological vector lattice has a closed positive cone and is thus an [[ordered topological vector space]].{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=234–242}} 
Let <math>\mathcal{B}</math> denote the set of all bounded subsets of a topological vector lattice with positive cone <math>C</math> and for any subset <math>S</math>, let <math>[S]_C := (S + C) \cap (S - C)</math> be the [[Cone-saturated|<math>C</math>-saturated]] hull of <math>S</math>. 
Then the topological vector lattice's positive cone <math>C</math> is a strict <math>\mathcal{B}</math>-cone,{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=234–242}} where <math>C</math> is a '''strict <math>\mathcal{B}</math>-cone''' means that <math>\left\{ [B]_C : B \in \mathcal{B} \right\}</math> is a fundamental subfamily of <math>\mathcal{B}</math> that is, every <math>B \in \mathcal{B}</math> is contained as a subset of some element of <math>\left\{ [B]_C : B \in \mathcal{B} \right\}</math>).{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=215–222}} 

If a topological vector lattice <math>X</math> is [[order complete]] then every band is closed in <math>X</math>.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=234–242}} 

== Examples ==

The [[Lp space|L<sup>p</sup> spaces]] (<math>1 \leq p \leq \infty</math>) are [[Banach lattice]]s under their canonical orderings. 
These spaces are order complete for <math>p < \infty</math>.
